chunks: "For the inverting amplifier I draw an op-amp with the plus input tied to ground.
The signal goes through an input resistor, R in , to the minus input, and a feedback resistor, R f , goes from the output back to the minus input.
The minus node is a virtual ground, so the input current is V in over R in , all of it flows through R f , and V out equals -(R f over R in)V in .
For the non-inverting amplifier, the signal goes straight into the plus input.
From the output I run a resistor divider to ground, R f on top and R g on the bottom, and the midpoint goes to the minus input.
The virtual short says the minus node equals V in , and that node is V outR g over (R g plus R f) , so V out equals (1 plus R f over R g)V in .
With R f equals 100 kilohms and 10 kilohms for the other resistor, the inverting amp gives minus 10 and the non-inverting amp gives plus 11.
Differences: the inverting circuit's input impedance is just R in , so it loads the source, while the non-inverting one has an extremely high input impedance.
Non-inverting can't give a gain below 1 and inverting can. Both have the same bandwidth for the same R f over R in ratio, since the loop gain is the same."
